title: Checkpoint: How Music Works
objective: After this level you can connect sound, pitch, rhythm, melody and harmony.
summary: One written A travels from the staff to a 440 Hz vibration, crosses the air as pressure waves and shakes the eardrum; inside the cochlea, each pitch has its own place, high near the wide end.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: follow one A from the page into your head.
cards.body: A single written note touches everything in this chapter. It starts as a dot on a staff, becomes a vibration, crosses the room and gets sorted inside your ear. Here's the trip, step by step, including one last stop you haven't met yet.

cards.headline: One A, from page to ear

events.label: Second space of the treble staff: the A above middle C
A string vibrates 440 times a second
Compressions and rarefactions travel about 343 m/s
The eardrum vibrates along with them
Hair cells in one spot respond to that pitch

cards.headline: Your inner ear is laid out like a keyboard
cards.body: Deep in your ear, the snail-shaped cochlea sorts sound by pitch. Hair cells near its wide end respond to high pitches, like a baby crying; those toward the center respond to low ones, like a big dog barking. Each pitch has its own neighborhood, a bit like keys along a piano. And remember Level 3: with age, it's usually the high pitches that fade first.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one breath
cards.body: Sound is air pressure, shaking. Pitch is how fast it shakes. Rhythm is when the sounds start and stop over a steady beat; melody is single notes strung into one line; harmony is notes sounding at the same time. Everything else in this chapter, from triads to octaves to the staff, is a way of organizing those shakes.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: How sound becomes music: vibrations in the air, organized into rhythm, melody and harmony.
Why a faster vibration sounds higher, and why a note an octave up sounds like the same note.
What separates beat, tempo and rhythm, and why a tune stays the same song from any starting note.
Why major often sounds bright and minor darker, and how much of that feeling is learned.

questions.prompt: Where in the cochlea do hair cells detect high-pitched sounds?

options.label: Near its center
options.rationale: Hair cells toward the center detect low pitches.

options.label: In the eardrum
options.rationale: The eardrum vibrates; it has no hair cells.

options.label: Everywhere equally
options.rationale: Each pitch has its own place.

questions.explanation: Hair cells near the wide end detect high pitches; those toward the center, low ones.

questions.prompt: An older listener misses a high beep but hears a low hum fine. What fits this chapter's ear science?

options.label: Low sounds travel faster through air
options.rationale: All pitches travel at the same speed.

options.label: The beep was below 20 Hz
options.rationale: A beep is high, not a deep rumble.

options.label: Age-related loss usually hits high pitches first
The eardrum only vibrates for low notes
options.rationale: The eardrum vibrates for all audible sounds.

questions.explanation: Different pitches are sensed in different places in the cochlea, and age usually takes the high end first.

questions.prompt: On this chapter's page-to-ear trip, what physically carries the A from the string to you?

options.label: Air molecules flying from the string to your ear
options.rationale: They jiggle in place and pass the push along.

options.label: Light from the vibrating string
options.rationale: Light isn't sound; sound needs a medium.

options.label: Electric signals in the air
options.rationale: Sound is mechanical: pressure, not electricity.

options.label: Compressions and rarefactions in the air

questions.explanation: Sound is a pressure wave: squeezes and thinnings of air, passed along at about 343 m/s.

questions.prompt: From Level 7's major and minor chords: which note moves when C major (C-E-G) becomes C minor?

options.label: E drops one semitone to E-flat
All three move up an octave
options.rationale: That changes register, not major to minor.

questions.explanation: Only the third moves: four semitones above the root in major, three in minor.

questions.prompt: From Level 8's octaves: how are an A at 220 Hz and an A at 440 Hz related?

options.label: A semitone apart, one key to the next
options.rationale: A semitone is a much smaller step.

options.label: The same pitch, just louder
options.rationale: One vibrates twice as fast, so it sounds higher.

options.label: A major third apart, four semitones
options.rationale: A major third is four semitones, not a doubling.

questions.explanation: An octave doubles the frequency, and notes an octave apart share a letter name.
